You are reverse-engineering a compiled binary by BEHAVIORAL OBSERVATION ONLY.

Binary: /workspace/executable  (a spaced-repetition CLI called "hashcards", version 0.3.0)
Docs: /workspace/README.md ; example collection: /tmp/explore/_example_master (copy it, never modify the master)

HARD RULES (violating these fails the whole task):
- NEVER decompile, disassemble, or inspect the binary bytes (no objdump, nm, strings, readelf, ghidra, gdb, hexdump on /workspace/executable).
- NEVER use strace/ltrace/perf or any tracing on /workspace/executable.
- NEVER search the internet or any package registry for the project source code. You have no network anyway.
- ONLY run the binary with CLI args / HTTP requests and observe stdout, stderr, exit codes, files it writes, and HTTP responses.

Environment: python3 (3.10, has sqlite3 module), curl, no network. Use python3 to inspect the hashcards.db SQLite file.

Working discipline:
- Work ONLY inside your own scratch dir (mkdir -p it).
- Write detailed findings to your findings file as you go. Be exhaustive and BYTE-EXACT: paste literal expected output, exact error strings, exact exit codes.
- Save large artifacts (full HTML/CSS/JS/JSON dumps) as separate files in a sibling directory and reference them.
- Your final returned text must be a dense, complete summary of the RULES you inferred (not a narration of what you tried). Someone must be able to reimplement from it.
- Prefer many small experiments. Test edge cases aggressively. When you see a rule, try to break it.

AREA: CLI surface / argument parsing (the binary uses a Rust clap-style parser).

Capture BYTE-EXACT text for:
- the binary with no args; --help; -h; --version; -V
- every subcommand with -h AND with --help (they differ: -h is the short summary, --help the long one): drill, check, stats, orphans, orphans list, orphans delete, export
- the help subcommand: help / help drill / help orphans / help orphans list / help help
- error cases: unknown subcommand, unknown flag, missing flag value, invalid value for --answer-controls / --format / --open-browser / --bury-siblings, non-numeric --port / --card-limit / --new-card-limit, out-of-range port (99999, -1, 0), too many positional args, bare -- handling, flag abbreviation (does --por 1 work?), equals-sign vs space form.
- exit codes for every case, and whether output goes to stdout or stderr.
- directory argument handling for check/stats/export/drill: nonexistent dir, a file instead of a dir, unreadable dir, empty dir, relative vs absolute path, trailing slash, dot and dot-dot, path with spaces. Record the EXACT error text and exit code.
Write everything with fenced literal blocks.

Your scratch dir is /tmp/explore/cli-surface. Write findings to /tmp/findings/cli-surface.md and artifacts under /tmp/findings/cli-surface/.

Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

Hashcards

A plain text-based spaced repetition system.

Features:
- Store flashcards as plain Markdown files (front/back and cloze cards supported).
- Content-addressable cards: cards are identified by the hash of their text.
- Low friction: edit cards with your editor of choice; use standard tools and VCS.
- Efficient scheduling using an established spaced-repetition algorithm.

Example deck (a Markdown file):

```
Q: How many neurons are there in the human brain?
A: ~80 billion.

C: An [agonist] is a ligand that binds to a receptor and [activates it].
```

Installation

Download a pre-built binary from the project's releases page: https://github.com/eudoxia0/hashcards/releases

Usage

Start a drilling session for a directory containing your Markdown decks:

```
$ hashcards drill [DIRECTORY]
```

Common commands

- drill [DIRECTORY]      Start a drilling session (launches a local web interface).
- stats [DIRECTORY]      Print collection statistics (JSON output supported).
- check [DIRECTORY]      Check integrity of a collection.
- orphans list|delete    Manage orphan cards in a collection.
- export [DIRECTORY]     Export a collection to JSON (prints to stdout by default).

Configuration & data

Runtime data (such as review progress) is stored in a collection database (e.g. an SQLite file) in the root of your card collection directory. This README intentionally omits implementation-specific details (internal schemas, build instructions, and developer notes).

For detailed user-oriented documentation and examples, see the example/ directory (if present) in this repository.

LICENSE

This project is distributed under the terms of the LICENSE file included in this repository.

cat > /tmp/explore/cli-surface/cap.py <<'PYEOF'
import subprocess, sys, os, json
BIN="/workspace/executable"
def run(args, cwd=None, stdin=b"", timeout=15, env=None):
    try:
        p=subprocess.run([BIN]+args, capture_output=True, input=stdin, cwd=cwd, timeout=timeout, env=env)
        return p.returncode, p.stdout, p.stderr
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as e:
        return "TIMEOUT", e.stdout or b"", e.stderr or b""
def show(args, cwd=None, label=None, timeout=15):
    rc,o,e = run(args, cwd=cwd, timeout=timeout)
    print("=== ARGV: %r%s" % (args, (" [cwd=%s]"%cwd) if cwd else ""))
    print("--- exit: %s" % rc)
    print("--- stdout (%d bytes):" % len(o))
    sys.stdout.write(o.decode("utf-8","replace"))
    if o and not o.endswith(b"\n"): print("<NO-TRAILING-NEWLINE>")
    print("--- stderr (%d bytes):" % len(e))
    sys.stdout.write(e.decode("utf-8","replace"))
    if e and not e.endswith(b"\n"): print("<NO-TRAILING-NEWLINE>")
    print("=== END\n")
if __name__=="__main__":
    import ast
    for line in sys.stdin:
        line=line.strip()
        if not line: continue
        show(ast.literal_eval(line))
PYEOF
